source_text: Sed dicet aliquis: Quomodo resurgunt mortui? Quo autem in corpore veniunt? Insipiens, tu quod seminas non vivificatur, nisi prius moriatur. Non omnis caro eadem caro; alia quidem hominis, alia pecoris; alia caro volatilium, alia autem piscium; et corpora caelestia et terrestria; sed alia quidem caelestium claritas, alia vero terrestrium; alia claritas solis, et alia claritas lunae, et alia claritas stellarum; stella enim a stella differt in gloria; ita et resurrectio mortuorum. Seminatur in corruptione, surget in incorruptela; seminatur in ignominia, surget in gloria; seminatur in infirmitate, surget in virtute; seminatur corpus animale, surget corpus spiritale. Sic etiam scriptum est: Factus est homo primus Adam in animam viventem, novissimus Adam in spiritum vivificantem. Primus homo de terra, terrestris; secundus homo de caelo, caelestis; qualis terrestris, tales et terreni; et qualis caelestis, tales et caelestes. Sicut portavimus imaginem terrestris, portemus etiam imaginem illius caelestis [n232] . Difficultatem rei exemplis edomat, et dicit nihil esse impossibile, cum omnipotentia pollicetur effectum. Sed sicut resurrectionem corporum seminum collatione commendat, ita etiam resurgentium diversitatem creaturarum varietatibus aperit; totum tamen loquitur de resurrectione beatorum. Seminatur - inquit - in ignominia, surget in gloria; seminatur in infirmitate, surget in virtute; seminatur corpus animale, surget corpus spiritale. Hoc certe nisi in sanctis impleri non potest; impii quoque non in gloriam excitantur, sed in opprobrium, sicut Propheta asserit, sempiternum [n233] . Hic opportune distantiam naturae atque gratiae facit, recordaturque testimonii veteris quo dictum est: Factus est homo primus Adam in animam viventem; subditque de suo: novissimus Adam in spiritum vivificantem. Ostenditque immortalitatis dona ad vivificantem spiritum pertinere; animam vero solum viventem, ad naturam quandoque morientem. Non est ergo, inquit, hoc vivens quod vivificans; vivificans est, qui confert immortalitatem, quam Christo applicat; vivens est autem, qui vita utitur, sed non excludit mortalitatem. Ergo hoc utramque sententiam fine discrevit, ut ostenderet Adam factum esse viventem, sed non immortalem; Christum autem in spiritum, non solum viventem, verum etiam conferentem resurrectionem, suis gloriosam, omnibus aeternam.
pass_a_gloss: But someone will say: How do the dead rise? But in what body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not made alive, unless first it dies. Not all flesh is the same flesh; one indeed of a human, another of cattle; another flesh of flying things, but another of fishes; and heavenly and earthly bodies; but one indeed the brightness of heavenly, but another of earthly; another the brightness of the sun, and another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of stars; for a star differs from a star in glory; so also the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in ignominy, it will rise in glory; it is sown in infirmity, it will rise in virtue; an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise. Thus also it is written: The first human Adam was made into a living soul, the last Adam into a life-giving spirit. The first human from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly; of what sort the earthly, such also the earthly; and of what sort the heavenly, such also the heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of that heavenly. He tames the difficulty of the matter by examples, and says nothing is impossible, when omnipotence promises an effect. But as he commends a resurrection of bodies by a comparison of seeds, so also he opens a diversity of those rising by varieties of creatures; yet he speaks the whole about a resurrection of the blessed. It is sown, he says, in ignominy, it will rise in glory; it is sown in infirmity, it will rise in virtue; an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise. This certainly cannot be fulfilled except in the holy; the impious also are not stirred into glory, but into an everlasting reproach, as the Prophet asserts. Here opportunely he makes a distance of nature and of grace, and remembers the old testimony by which it was said: The first human Adam was made into a living soul; and he subjoins from his own: the last Adam into a life-giving spirit. And he showed that the gifts of immortality belong to a life-giving spirit; but a soul only living, to a nature sometime dying. It is not therefore, he says, this living which is life-giving; life-giving is he who confers immortality, which he applies to Christ; but living is he who uses life, but does not exclude mortality. Therefore he distinguished each sentence by this end, that he might show Adam was made living, but not immortal; but Christ into a spirit, not only living, but even conferring a resurrection, glorious for his own, eternal for all.

pass_b_english: ‘But someone will say: How do the dead rise? In what body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. Not all flesh is the same: human flesh is one kind, animals’ (Daniel 12:2) another; birds’ flesh one kind, fish another. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of heavenly bodies differs from the glory of earthly bodies. The sun has one glory, the moon another, and the stars another, for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

‘It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; sown in weakness, it will rise in power; sown an animate body, it will rise a spiritual body. Thus it is also written: The first human, Adam, became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly. As the earthly one is, so are earthly people; as the heavenly one is, so are heavenly people. As we have borne the earthly one’s image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image’ (1 Corinthians 15:35–49).

He masters the difficulty through examples, saying that nothing is impossible when omnipotence promises the result. Just as he commends bodily resurrection through comparison with seeds, he explains differences among those rising through the variety of creatures. Yet throughout he speaks of the blessed’s resurrection. ‘It is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; sown in weakness, it will rise in power; sown an animate body, it will rise a spiritual body.’ This can certainly be fulfilled only in the saints. The ungodly are raised not into glory but into everlasting disgrace, as the prophet declares (compare Jeremiah 23:40; Daniel 12:2).

Here he appropriately distinguishes nature and grace, recalling the old testimony: ‘The first human, Adam, became a living soul’ (Genesis 2:7), then adding in his own words, ‘The last Adam a life-giving spirit.’ He shows that immortality’s gifts belong to the life-giving spirit, while a soul that merely lives belongs to a nature that will one day die. Living, then, he says, is not the same as life-giving. The life-giving one bestows immortality, which he assigns to Christ; the living one enjoys life but does not exclude mortality. He distinguished the two statements for this purpose: to show Adam was made living, but not immortal, while Christ became a spirit not merely living but bestowing resurrection—glorious for his own people, everlasting for everyone.
